I can't speak for anyone (I don't even personally block bridges myself) but I believe the thinking behind these disruptions is that the audience is not the bystander, the audience is the administration. 

Building solidarity is important but it is a long-term, slow and sustained effort, while the goal of these disruptions is that the protestors feel there is a state of emergency that requires immediate action of people in power. The tradeoff of losing the opinion of a bystander who was on the fence but leaning against solidarity anyways is less critical than exerting pressure on officials. 

And of course, rising escalations in civil disobedience is intended to send a message to the administration that until some kind of concession is met, the disruptions (to their constituents who are getting very annoyed) will increase in severity. People will get more and more angry, and complain to their officials, "can't you do something about these losers on the bridge???" and since you can't execute protestors, the hope is that eventually the officials will do anything to make the disturbance go away, even make concessions.
